meanings.short: The working assumption that, on large enough scales, the universe is the same at every place and in every direction.
meanings.long: In words: the universe is homogeneous and isotropic once we average over regions hundreds of millions of light-years across. From it alone one can show that any expansion must follow Hubble's law, with speed proportional to distance.

meanings.short: Moving along with the expansion of the universe, or measured on a grid that stretches with it, so the expansion itself is divided out.
meanings.long: A comoving observer is at rest relative to the matter around it. A comoving density is the number per comoving volume: it stays fixed when particles are only diluted by the expansion, and changes only when they are made or destroyed.

meanings.short: The result that, in a spherically symmetric spread of matter, the matter outside a sphere has no gravitational effect on what is inside it.
meanings.long: In Newtonian form: for a spherically symmetric distribution, the force on a sphere depends only on the mass inside it. So a uniform sphere cut from the universe expands just like the whole, and a simple Newtonian argument gives the Friedmann equation. The general-relativity version says the field outside any spherical mass is the Schwarzschild field.

meanings.short: How much a curve, a surface or a space bends away from being straight or flat.
meanings.long: A curve's curvature is one over the radius of the circle that best fits it. For space, curvature shows up in geometry: on a positively curved space, like a sphere, the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees; on a negatively curved one, to less. In cosmology the curvature term of the Friedmann equation decides, with the density, whether the universe is open, flat or closed.

meanings.short: A model universe that is flat and contains only matter, which expands for ever while slowing down.
meanings.long: Its scale factor grows as the two-thirds power of time, and its density always equals the critical density. It is the simplest background for calculations of how structure grows, and a fair description of our universe between about 50,000 years and a few billion years after the Big Bang.

meanings.short: A model universe with no matter or energy at all, only negative curvature, which expands at a constant rate.
meanings.long: With nothing to slow it, the scale factor grows in proportion to time. It is a limiting case of an open universe, and a useful comparison for models with matter or a cosmological constant.

meanings.short: The combination of curvature quantities that forms the left side of Einstein's field equations, describing how spacetime is curved.
meanings.long: It is built from the first and second derivatives of the metric. Einstein's equations set it equal to 8πG/c⁴ times the stress–energy tensor (plus a cosmological constant term): the geometry on one side, the matter and energy on the other.

meanings.short: A table of ten numbers at each point that describes all the energy, momentum, pressure and stress there; it is what curves spacetime.
meanings.long: Its time–time entry is the energy density, the mixed entries the flow of energy and the momentum density, and the space–space entries the pressures and shear stresses. In Einstein's equations it is the source of gravity, as mass density is in Poisson's equation.

meanings.short: A fluid described completely by its density and a pressure that is the same in every direction, with no viscosity or heat flow.
meanings.long: In its rest frame its stress–energy tensor has the energy density in the first slot and the same pressure p in each of the three space directions, and zeros elsewhere. The matter, radiation and vacuum energy of a uniform universe are all treated as perfect fluids.

meanings.short: A density divided by the critical density, written Ω; one for each ingredient, such as matter, radiation and dark energy.
meanings.long: Today Ω for matter is about 0.3 and for the cosmological constant about 0.7. The values add up to one exactly when space is flat; what is left over is the curvature term, Ωₖ.

meanings.short: The moment, about 50,000 years after the Big Bang, when matter and radiation had the same energy density; after it matter dominated.
meanings.long: Radiation thins out as the fourth power of the scale factor, matter only as the third, so radiation dominates early and matter later. In the 8.902 notes equality is at a redshift of about 3200.

meanings.short: The moment, a few billion years ago, when the density of matter fell to that of the cosmological constant; since then dark energy dominates.
meanings.long: Matter thins out as the expansion proceeds, while a cosmological constant keeps the same density. For today's values the two were equal at a redshift of about 0.3.

meanings.short: The early period of the universe, after inflation and up to about 50,000 years, when radiation outweighed matter and set the rate of expansion.
meanings.long: During it the scale factor grew as the square root of time. Dark matter clumps that entered the horizon then hardly grew, because the expansion was faster than their collapse.

meanings.short: The slowing effect of the expansion of the universe, which acts like friction on a rolling field or a growing clump.
meanings.long: In the equation for a scalar field it is the term 3H times the field's rate of change; in the growth of density ripples a similar term turns exponential growth into a slow power law. In a static universe there is no Hubble drag.

meanings.short: The phase of inflation in which the field drifts slowly down a nearly flat potential, so its energy is almost all potential energy.
meanings.long: While the field's kinetic energy is small compared with its potential energy, its pressure is close to minus its energy density and the universe expands almost exponentially. Inflation ends when the field speeds up near the bottom of the potential.

meanings.short: Two small numbers, ε and η, that measure the slope and the bending of an inflation potential; inflation needs both to be small.
meanings.long: ε depends on the square of V′/V, η on V″/V. When both are much less than one the field rolls slowly and inflation continues; when they approach one it ends.

meanings.short: Expansion of the universe that gets faster with time, so the distance between far-apart galaxies grows ever more quickly.
meanings.long: Mathematically, the second time derivative of the scale factor is positive. The second Friedmann equation shows that this needs a pressure more negative than minus one third of the energy density times c². Inflation was an early era of accelerated expansion; dark energy drives the present one.

meanings.short: The tiny density ripples in the early universe from which galaxies and clusters later grew.
meanings.long: Inflation stretches quantum fluctuations to enormous sizes, leaving ripples of about one part in 100,000. Gravity then amplifies them into the structure we see.

meanings.short: The distance found by dividing an object's true size by the angle it covers on the sky.
meanings.long: In an expanding universe it differs from the luminosity distance by a factor (1 + z)²: the angular diameter distance is the comoving distance divided by 1 + z. Beyond a redshift of about 1.6, more distant objects of the same size look larger, not smaller.

meanings.short: The distance between two objects measured on the stretching grid of comoving coordinates, which does not change as the universe expands.
meanings.long: It is today's distance between two points that move with the expansion. Light from redshift z has crossed a comoving distance equal to the integral of c dz/H(z); the angular diameter and luminosity distances are built from it.

meanings.short: A volume measured in comoving coordinates, which stays the same as the universe expands; counts per comoving volume remove the effect of expansion.
meanings.long: Astronomers convert numbers of galaxies counted in a patch of sky between two redshifts into a density by dividing by the comoving volume of that slice. A slice's comoving volume is its area at the time times (1 + z)², times its comoving depth.

meanings.short: The magnitude a star or galaxy would have if it were 10 parsecs away: a measure of its true brightness.
meanings.long: The difference between apparent and absolute magnitude, the distance modulus, depends only on distance: m − M = 5 log(D/10 pc). A typical bright galaxy has an absolute magnitude of about −21.

meanings.short: How bright an object looks from Earth, on the astronomers' magnitude scale, where a larger number means fainter.
meanings.long: Two objects differ in apparent magnitude by −2.5 times the base-10 logarithm of the ratio of their fluxes: 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100. The zero point is set by a reference, the Vega or the AB system.

meanings.short: A magnitude scale whose zero point is the bright star Vega: Vega has magnitude zero in every filter.
meanings.long: Because Vega's spectrum is not flat, the reference flux differs from filter to filter. It is the traditional system of optical astronomy.

meanings.short: A magnitude scale whose zero point is an imagined source giving the same flux per unit frequency at every frequency.
meanings.long: The reference is 3.63 × 10⁻²⁰ erg per second per square centimetre per hertz, so a source of that flux density has AB magnitude zero in any filter. Large surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey use it.

meanings.short: A magnitude measured through a filter, from all the light the filter lets through, rather than at one frequency.
meanings.long: It compares the flux integrated over the filter's transmission with that of the reference source through the same filter. The U, B, V, R, I filters and the u, g, r, i, z filters of the Sloan survey each give their own band magnitude.

meanings.short: A magnitude measured at a single frequency or wavelength, rather than through a filter.
meanings.long: It is −2.5 times the logarithm of the flux per unit frequency divided by that of the reference source at the same frequency. In practice light is always collected through a filter, so band magnitudes are what is measured.

everyday: In astronomy a colour is a number, a difference of two magnitudes; for quarks it is a kind of charge with nothing to do with light.

meanings.short: A kind of charge carried by quarks, with three values, on which the strong force acts; it has nothing to do with visible colour.
meanings.long: Each flavour of quark comes in three colours, often named red, green and blue. The strong force treats them symmetrically, and the gluons carry colour between quarks; only colourless combinations, such as the three quarks of a proton, exist freely.

meanings.short: In astronomy, the difference between an object's magnitudes in two filters; a larger value means redder light.
meanings.long: For filters X and Y the colour is m_X − m_Y. It does not depend on distance, because distance dims both bands equally. A larger g − r means relatively less blue light, so a redder object, usually an older stellar population.

meanings.short: How bright an extended object such as a galaxy is per unit area of sky, usually in magnitudes per square arcsecond.
meanings.long: Because both the flux and the area on the sky fall as the inverse square of distance, surface brightness does not change with distance in a static universe. In an expanding one it falls as (1 + z) to the fourth power. Lensing leaves it unchanged.

meanings.short: The energy of light arriving per second, per unit area, per unit frequency and per unit solid angle of sky.
meanings.long: It is the flux per solid angle. Since flux and solid angle both fall as the inverse square of distance, specific intensity is the same at any distance from a source, which is why a nearby and a distant wall look equally bright.

meanings.short: A formula for how a galaxy's surface brightness falls off from its centre, with one number, the index n, setting the shape.
meanings.long: The brightness falls as e to the power −(r/r₀)^(1/n). An index of 1 gives the exponential profile of discs; 4 gives the de Vaucouleurs profile of ellipticals, with a sharp bright centre and a wide faint envelope.

meanings.short: The way the surface brightness of an elliptical galaxy falls with radius: as an exponential of the quarter power of radius.
meanings.long: It is the Sérsic profile with index 4. It has a bright, cusped centre and an envelope that fades slowly to large radii.

meanings.short: A galaxy with a flat, rotating disc of stars and gas, usually with spiral arms, young stars and blue colours.
meanings.long: Spirals (Sp) are most common away from clusters. Their stars and gas are held up mainly by rotation, and their brightness falls exponentially from the centre. The Milky Way and Andromeda are spirals.

meanings.short: A smooth, rounded galaxy of old, red stars moving in random directions, with little gas and little rotation.
meanings.long: Ellipticals (E) are most common in clusters. They are held up by the random motions of their stars, their velocity dispersion, rather than by rotation, and follow the de Vaucouleurs profile. M87 is one.

origin: Latin lenticula, a lentil, from its lens shape.

meanings.short: A galaxy with a disc of stars but no gas disc or spiral arms, in between spirals and ellipticals.
meanings.long: Lenticulars are labelled S0. Like spirals they have a disc; like ellipticals they have mostly old stars and little gas. NGC 2787 is an example.

meanings.short: A formula for how many galaxies there are of each brightness: a power law for faint galaxies with a sharp cut-off above a typical brightness.
meanings.long: The number per luminosity interval goes as (L/L*) to a power α times e to the power −L/L*. Faint galaxies are numerous; galaxies much brighter than L* are exponentially rare. It also fits the numbers of galaxies of each stellar mass.

meanings.short: The number of galaxies (or stars) per unit volume in each range of luminosity.
meanings.long: It is usually fitted by a Schechter function. A conditional luminosity function gives the same count for galaxies in halos of one mass.

meanings.short: How the light of a star or galaxy is spread over wavelengths, for example from ultraviolet to infrared.
meanings.long: A galaxy's spectral energy distribution (SED) is the sum of the light of all its stars, plus gas and dust. Fitting it with stars of different types and ages tells what the galaxy is made of.

meanings.short: Working out which stars make up a galaxy by building its spectrum from the spectra of many kinds of star and matching the result.
meanings.long: One chooses an initial mass function and a star formation history, adds up the spectra of the stars these produce, and compares the total with the observed spectrum. It gives the ages, metallicities and stellar mass of the galaxy, with some degeneracies.

meanings.short: The stars of a galaxy or a part of it, described by their ages, chemical make-up and masses.
meanings.long: A young population is blue and bright, dominated by short-lived massive stars; an old one is red and dim. A simple stellar population has stars all of one age and one metallicity.

origin: Latin co-, together, and aevum, age.

meanings.short: Of the same age; a coeval population is a group of stars all born at the same time.
meanings.long: A coeval population (also called a simple stellar population) is the building block of population synthesis: a galaxy's light is a sum of coeval populations born at different times. Its light changes in a predictable way as it ages and its most massive stars die.

meanings.short: The mass of new stars a galaxy makes per unit time, usually in solar masses per year.
meanings.long: It is measured from the light of young massive stars: their ultraviolet light, the Hα line of gas they ionise, and far-infrared light from dust they heat. The Milky Way forms a few solar masses of stars per year.

meanings.short: The share of newborn stars of each mass: how many stars form at each mass when a population is born.
meanings.long: Low-mass stars are far more numerous than massive ones. The IMF is often taken as Salpeter's power law; other forms flatten below one solar mass. A bottom-heavy IMF has extra low-mass stars, a top-heavy one extra massive stars.

meanings.short: The initial mass function found by Edwin Salpeter in 1955: the number of stars per unit mass falls as mass to the power −2.35.
meanings.long: It describes stars above about one solar mass well. Below that it gives too many faint stars compared with later forms, such as those of Chabrier and Kroupa, so it predicts a higher mass-to-light ratio.

everyday: Astronomers call every element heavier than helium a metal, including oxygen and carbon.

meanings.short: The fraction of a star's or gas cloud's mass in elements heavier than helium, which astronomers call metals.
meanings.long: It is written Z; the Sun's is about 0.02. Stars make metals and supernovae spread them, so the metallicity of gas rises with time and acts as a clock for a galaxy's history.

meanings.short: How much of something there is, such as a chemical element, a kind of particle, or objects like clusters, usually compared with something else.
meanings.long: Astronomers give the abundance of one element relative to another as a logarithm compared with the Sun: [Fe/H] = −1 means one tenth of the Sun's ratio of iron to hydrogen. In cosmology the abundances of the light elements and of dark matter particles are set in the first minutes and earlier.

meanings.short: The gradual build-up of heavy elements in a galaxy as generations of stars make them and return them to the gas.
meanings.long: Models follow the mass of gas and its metallicity as stars form, gas flows in or out and dying stars return enriched material. The simplest is the closed box.

meanings.short: The simplest model of a galaxy's chemical evolution: a fixed amount of gas, with nothing flowing in or out, slowly turned into stars.
meanings.long: Starting from metal-free gas, it predicts that the gas metallicity equals the yield times the logarithm of one over the gas fraction. It predicts too many metal-poor long-lived stars, the G-dwarf problem, so real galaxies are not closed boxes.

meanings.short: The simplifying assumption that massive stars return their new elements to the gas at once, and light stars never.
meanings.long: It works because massive stars live only a few million years, short compared with a galaxy's history. It makes the equations of chemical evolution solvable by hand.

meanings.short: An ordinary star like the Sun, of spectral type G, still burning hydrogen in its core.
meanings.long: G dwarfs live about ten billion years, longer than the age of the Galaxy's disc, so every one ever formed is still shining. Their metallicities therefore record the whole history of the gas they formed from.

meanings.short: The finding that there are far fewer metal-poor Sun-like stars nearby than the closed-box model of chemical evolution predicts.
meanings.long: It shows that the Galaxy's disc was not a closed box: fresh gas kept flowing in, or the first stars formed differently. Models with gas flowing in over time fit the observed metallicities much better.

meanings.short: Infrared light of long wavelength, roughly 25 to 350 micrometres, such as the glow of cool dust.
meanings.long: Dust around young stars absorbs their ultraviolet light and re-emits it in the far-infrared, so far-infrared brightness measures star formation that is hidden from optical telescopes. Molecules also absorb and emit it as they change their rotation.

meanings.short: A red spectral line of hydrogen, at 656 nanometres, given off when an electron drops from the third to the second level.
meanings.long: Gas ionised by young massive stars glows strongly in Hα, so its brightness measures how fast a galaxy is forming stars. It is the first line of the Balmer series, in which electrons fall to the second level.

meanings.short: Light with wavelengths shorter than violet, from about 10 to 400 nanometres, invisible to the eye.
meanings.long: Young massive stars, quasars and the gas near them give off most of their light in the ultraviolet. Ultraviolet photons with more than 13.6 electronvolts can ionise hydrogen.

meanings.short: The sum, over all particles of a system, of each particle's momentum times its position, used to derive the virial theorem.
meanings.long: Its time derivative equals twice the kinetic energy plus a sum of forces times positions. For a system in a steady state its time average does not change, which gives the virial theorem.

meanings.short: For a bound system in a steady state, a fixed link between average kinetic and potential energy; for gravity, 2T + U = 0.
meanings.long: In symbols 2T + U = 0, averaged over time. It lets astronomers weigh a galaxy or cluster from how fast its stars or galaxies move and how big it is. The total energy, half the potential energy, is negative, as it must be for a bound system.

meanings.short: The settled state of a bound system whose kinetic and potential energies obey the virial theorem; to virialise is to reach it.
meanings.long: A collapsing dark matter halo does not shrink to a point: random motions build up until 2T + U = 0. In the spherical collapse model the virialised halo is about 18π², or 178, times denser than the background.

meanings.short: A relation in which one quantity is proportional to another raised to a fixed power, such as y ∝ x³.
meanings.long: On a graph with logarithmic axes a power law is a straight line whose slope is the power. Many relations in astronomy, such as Tully–Fisher or the Salpeter initial mass function, are power laws over a wide range.

meanings.short: In a system of stars, the time after which the small gravitational tugs of neighbours have changed a star's speed completely.
meanings.long: It is about N/(6 ln N) crossing times for N stars. For a galaxy, with about a hundred billion stars, it is far longer than the age of the universe, so galaxies are effectively collisionless; in dense globular clusters it is much shorter.

meanings.short: Of a galaxy or cluster: settled into a steady state, so its smoothed distribution of stars in position and speed no longer changes.
meanings.long: Stars almost never collide, yet galaxies relax within the age of the universe, through phase mixing and violent relaxation rather than encounters. To a first approximation, a relaxed system keeps no memory of how it formed apart from its total mass, energy and angular momentum.

meanings.short: Averaged over small cells, so fine details are smoothed away and only the broad pattern is kept.
meanings.long: The coarse-grained distribution of stars in phase space can become smooth and steady even though the exact, fine-grained distribution keeps winding into finer spirals. Observations always see the coarse-grained picture, since no telescope resolves every fine detail.

meanings.short: The spreading of a clump of stars along their orbits, because stars on slightly different orbits go round at different rates.
meanings.long: A compact group in phase space is sheared into a thin spiral that winds ever tighter. Smoothed over small cells the distribution then looks steady, so phase mixing helps a system relax without any collisions.

meanings.short: The rapid settling of a collapsing galaxy or halo, in which the quickly changing gravity reshuffles the energies of all its stars.
meanings.long: A star's energy changes only when the potential changes with time. During a collapse the potential changes fast, so energies are mixed within a few crossing times, much faster than encounters between stars could do it.

meanings.short: The logarithm of the ratio of the largest to the smallest distance at which encounters matter, written ln Λ; it counts distant weak encounters.
meanings.long: Adding up gravitational kicks from passing stars over all impact distances gives an integral of db/b, the logarithm of b_max/b_min. For a galaxy it is about 25. The same integral appears for charged particles in a plasma, hence the name.

meanings.short: A close pass between two stars that changes the speed of one by about as much as the speed itself, turning its path sharply.
meanings.long: In a galaxy a star suffers a strong encounter practically never; in dense globular clusters they are more common. Weak encounters, each a tiny nudge, are far more frequent and add up over time.

meanings.short: A dense, round cluster of tens of thousands to millions of old stars, orbiting a galaxy.
meanings.long: Globular clusters are among the oldest objects known, about 12 billion years old. Their stars move fast enough that their masses agree with the stars alone: they need no dark matter.

meanings.short: Unchanged by any rotation about one axis, like a disc or a spinning top.
meanings.long: An axisymmetric potential depends only on the distance from the axis and the height above the plane, not on the angle around the axis. Disc galaxies are modelled this way, and angular momentum about the axis is then conserved.

meanings.short: The same in every direction from a centre, so it depends only on the distance from that centre.
meanings.long: A spherically symmetric mass distribution has a density ρ(r) only. Its gravity outside any radius depends only on the mass inside, which makes it one of the easiest cases to calculate.

meanings.short: The point moving on a perfect circular orbit about which a star on a nearly circular orbit makes its small oscillations.
meanings.long: A star with the same angular momentum but a little more energy than a circular orbit wobbles in and out around its guiding centre, tracing a small ellipse, the epicycle. For the Sun the guiding centre lies about 8 kiloparsecs from the Galaxy's centre.

origin: Greek epi, upon, and kyklos, circle.

meanings.short: The small ellipse a star traces around its guiding centre when its orbit in a galaxy is nearly circular.
meanings.long: The radial oscillation has its own frequency κ, the epicycle frequency, which differs from the orbital frequency. Near the Sun a star goes round its epicycle about 1.3 times per orbit, so orbits in a galaxy do not close.

meanings.short: The rate at which a star in a disc galaxy bobs up and down through the plane of the disc.
meanings.long: Expanding the effective potential near the plane gives a simple harmonic oscillation in height with frequency ν, set by the density of the disc. It is usually different from both the orbital and the epicycle frequency.

meanings.short: An orbit at constant distance from the centre, where gravity supplies exactly the needed inward force.
meanings.long: Its speed v satisfies v²/r = the gravitational acceleration at r. Plotted against radius, the circular speed is a galaxy's rotation curve.

meanings.short: Two numbers, A and B, that describe how the Milky Way's rotation changes near the Sun, measured from the motions of nearby stars.
meanings.long: Differential rotation makes nearby stars show a pattern in their radial and sideways motions that varies with galactic longitude. A measures the shear of the rotation and B its local spin; together they give the epicycle frequency near the Sun.

meanings.short: A way of giving positions on the sky by longitude and latitude measured from the plane and centre of the Milky Way.
meanings.long: Longitude l is measured along the Galaxy's plane from the direction of its centre; latitude b is the angle above or below the plane. The Galactic centre is at l = 0, b = 0.

meanings.short: The finding that a spiral galaxy's luminosity grows as roughly the fourth power of its maximum rotation speed.
meanings.long: Found by Brent Tully and Richard Fisher in 1977, it lets astronomers find a spiral's luminosity, and so its distance, from its rotation speed. The exponent depends a little on the filter used.

meanings.short: The finding that an elliptical galaxy's luminosity grows as roughly the fourth power of the velocity dispersion of its stars.
meanings.long: It is the counterpart for ellipticals of the Tully–Fisher relation for spirals, with random speeds in place of rotation speed. Sandra Faber and Robert Jackson found it in 1976.

meanings.short: A mass distribution together with the gravitational potential it produces, linked by Poisson's equation.
meanings.long: Given the density one can find the potential by integration, and given the potential one finds the density from its Laplacian divided by 4πG. Known pairs, such as the point mass, the uniform sphere and the NFW halo, are the building blocks of galaxy models.

meanings.short: An infinitely thin disc whose surface density falls as one over radius, which gives the same rotation speed at every radius.
meanings.long: It shows that a flat rotation curve can come from a disc alone, without a spherical halo. Leon Mestel described it in 1963.

meanings.short: An amount of mass, charge or particles per unit area of a thin layer or surface.
meanings.long: For a galaxy disc it is the mass per unit area, written Σ, found by adding up the density through the disc's thickness, often in solar masses per square parsec. With the disc's random speeds it decides whether the disc is stable against clumping.

meanings.short: Another name for the divergence theorem: the total outward flow through a closed surface equals the total of the divergence inside it.
meanings.long: Applied to gravity it says that the flux of the gravitational field through a closed surface is −4πG times the mass enclosed. For a uniform sphere this gives the force at once, without integrating over the mass.

meanings.short: Here: the fact that a small enough patch of any smooth curved space looks flat, which the lesson credits to Gauss.
meanings.long: Near any point, a curved space can be described by ordinary flat (Euclidean) geometry, with corrections that grow with the square of the distance. The curvature shows up only over larger regions.

meanings.short: The density profile of simulated dark matter halos: rising as one over radius near the centre, falling as one over radius cubed far out.
meanings.long: Julio Navarro, Carlos Frenk and Simon White found in 1996 that halos of every mass share it: ρ = ρ₀ divided by (r/a)(1 + r/a)². Its shape is set by one extra number, the concentration, which depends only weakly on mass.

meanings.short: Of a dark matter halo: its outer radius divided by its scale radius; a large value means the mass is packed towards the centre.
meanings.long: It is usually r₂₀₀ over the scale radius. Halos that formed earlier, when the universe was denser, are more concentrated, so more massive halos, which form later, are less concentrated.

meanings.short: The central region of a star, galaxy, halo or cluster; for a halo, a centre where the density levels off instead of rising steeply.
meanings.long: A cored profile has a central slope near zero, unlike the cusp of simulated cold dark matter halos, whose density keeps rising as one over radius. Many dwarf and low surface brightness galaxies appear to have cores.

meanings.short: The mismatch between the steeply rising central densities of simulated dark matter halos and the flat cores many real galaxies seem to have.
meanings.long: Proposed answers fall into two families: ordinary matter, through supernova or black-hole feedback, pushes dark matter out of the centre; or dark matter is not quite cold and collisionless (warm, self-interacting or fuzzy). It is one of the main small-scale challenges to the standard cold dark matter model.

meanings.short: The finding that simulations of cold dark matter predict many more small subhalos around a galaxy like ours than there are satellite galaxies.
meanings.long: Simulations predict about a thousand subhalos around the Milky Way where about fifty satellites are known. Either many subhalos hold no stars, being dark, or dark matter erases small structures. Deeper surveys have closed part of the gap.

meanings.short: The puzzle that the largest predicted subhalos are too massive to have failed to form stars, yet no bright galaxies match them.
meanings.long: Their gravity should have held on to gas and made bright satellites, but the observed satellites have less dense centres than these subhalos. It sharpens the missing satellites problem, since dark subhalos cannot explain it.

meanings.short: The puzzle that real rotation curves come in many shapes, some cuspy and some cored, while simulated halos all look alike when scaled.
meanings.long: Galaxies of similar mass can have very different inner rotation curves. Since simulated halos follow one universal profile, the variety must come from ordinary matter or from the nature of dark matter.

meanings.short: Dark matter made of particles that moved slowly in the early universe, so small clumps could form first and merge into larger ones.
meanings.long: Its particles had tiny random speeds and feel only gravity, so its Jeans mass is tiny and it could start clumping before recombination, giving the seeds into which ordinary matter later fell. It is the CDM of the standard ΛCDM model.

meanings.short: Dark matter made of particles that moved at nearly light speed when structure began to form, such as light neutrinos.
meanings.long: Fast particles stream out of small clumps and smooth them away, so only very large structures could form first and would then have to break up into galaxies. Observations rule it out as the main dark matter.

meanings.short: Dark matter whose particles moved fast enough early on to erase the smallest clumps, but slowly enough to allow galaxies.
meanings.long: A particle of a few kiloelectronvolts, such as a sterile neutrino, would suppress halos below about a billion solar masses. It could ease the missing satellites and core–cusp problems while keeping the large-scale success of cold dark matter.

meanings.short: Dark matter whose particles can collide with one another much more than with ordinary matter, so dense halo centres spread into cores.
meanings.long: Collisions carry energy outwards from the centre of a halo and flatten its cusp. Galaxy cluster collisions such as the Bullet Cluster put an upper limit on how often the particles may scatter.

meanings.short: The escape of fast particles from small clumps, which smooths out all density ripples smaller than the distance they can travel.
meanings.long: The free-streaming length is the scale below which this wipes out structure: for hot dark matter it is huge, for cold dark matter tiny. It works like the Jeans length, with the particle speed in place of the sound speed.

meanings.short: Of structure formation: the largest structures form first and later break up into smaller ones, as hot dark matter would require.
meanings.long: Observations of galaxy clustering, the ages of galaxies and the Lyman-α forest rule it out in favour of bottom-up formation. It is what hot dark matter would give, because only very large clumps survive its free-streaming.

meanings.short: Of structure formation: small objects form first and merge into ever larger ones, as cold dark matter predicts.
meanings.long: Small halos collapse first because small scales carry the largest density ripples; they then fall into larger halos, some surviving inside as subhalos. It is the order seen in simulations of cold dark matter and supported by observations.

meanings.short: Of structure formation: built up step by step, small objects first, each larger one assembled from smaller ones.
meanings.long: In cold dark matter the density ripples are largest on small scales, so small halos collapse first and merge, making a tree of mergers for every large halo. Each halo's history can therefore be drawn as a merger tree.

meanings.short: In nested levels: each cell split into smaller cells, and those into smaller ones again.
Of particles in the early universe: to stop being made and destroyed once they become too rare to meet, leaving a fixed number behind.
meanings.long: While the reactions are faster than the expansion the particles stay in thermal equilibrium and grow rarer as the universe cools. Once the time between collisions exceeds the expansion time, reactions stop and the comoving number freezes at its value then, the relic abundance.

meanings.short: Of a mode of vibration: to stop sharing the thermal energy, because its smallest energy step is far above the typical thermal energy.
Of the forces of nature: to settle into their separate low-temperature forms as the early universe cooled.
The number of particles of a kind left over from the early universe after they froze out, which survives to today.
meanings.long: Particles that annihilate more readily freeze out later and leave fewer relics: the relic density is roughly inversely proportional to the annihilation rate. Matching it to the amount of dark matter is the WIMP miracle.

meanings.short: A kind of particle left over from the early universe: hot if still near light speed when it froze out, cold if already slow.
meanings.long: Light neutrinos are the classic hot relic and would be hot dark matter. Particles of about 100 GeV freeze out when already slow and are cold relics, cold dark matter.

meanings.short: Weakly interacting massive particle: a proposed dark matter particle of roughly 100 times a proton's mass, feeling only gravity and the weak force.
meanings.long: WIMPs would freeze out in the early universe with about the right abundance to be the dark matter, and particle theories such as supersymmetry offer candidates. Decades of searches underground, at colliders and in space have not found one.

meanings.short: The coincidence that a particle with weak-force interactions and a mass near 100 GeV would freeze out with just the observed amount of dark matter.
meanings.long: Working backwards from the dark matter density gives the annihilation rate needed, and it lands at the electroweak scale, where particle physicists had proposed new particles for other reasons. The miracle has guided most searches, so far without a detection.

meanings.short: The energy of about 100 GeV at which the electromagnetic and weak forces merge, set by the masses of the W, Z and Higgs bosons.
meanings.long: Particles with masses and interactions at this scale are natural in many extensions of the Standard Model, which is why WIMPs were expected there. It is far below the energy of grand unification, but within reach of the Large Hadron Collider.

meanings.short: The theory of the known particles and of three of the four forces: electromagnetism and the weak and strong nuclear forces.
meanings.long: It describes six quarks and six leptons, the force carriers (photon, gluons, W and Z bosons) and the Higgs boson, with symmetry group SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1). It agrees with every collider experiment so far, but contains no dark matter particle and leaves out gravity.

meanings.short: One of the basic particles that make up protons, neutrons and other hadrons; quarks are never found alone.
meanings.long: There are six kinds, or flavours: up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom. A proton is two up quarks and a down, a neutron two downs and an up. Quarks carry colour charge and are bound by gluons through the strong force.

meanings.short: Any particle made of quarks held together by the strong force, such as a proton, a neutron or a pion.
meanings.long: Hadrons are either baryons, made of three quarks, or mesons, made of a quark and an antiquark. In the early universe, about a hundred thousandth of a second after the Big Bang, free quarks and gluons were bound into hadrons.

everyday: Cosmologists use 'baryons' loosely for all ordinary matter, electrons included.

meanings.short: A particle made of three quarks, such as a proton or a neutron; in cosmology, ordinary matter as opposed to dark matter.
meanings.long: Since almost all the mass of ordinary matter is in protons and neutrons, astronomers call gas, stars and planets baryonic matter. Baryons make up about a sixth of all matter; the rest is dark.

origin: Greek mesos, middle, since the first ones found weigh between an electron and a proton.

meanings.short: A particle made of a quark and an antiquark, such as the pion; all mesons are unstable.
meanings.long: Mesons are hadrons with whole-number spin. The pion, the lightest, carries part of the force that binds protons and neutrons in a nucleus.

meanings.short: The antiparticle of the electron: the same mass, but a positive electric charge.
meanings.long: A positron and an electron that meet annihilate, usually into two gamma-ray photons. In the early universe electrons and positrons annihilated as it cooled below about a billion kelvin, heating the photons and leaving the small excess of electrons we see today.

meanings.short: A large, roughly round cloud of dark matter, held together by its own gravity, inside which a galaxy or a cluster of galaxies sits.
meanings.long: Halos form where the density was a little higher than average: the region stops expanding, collapses and settles into virial equilibrium. A galaxy's halo extends far beyond its stars and holds most of its mass.

meanings.short: The moment when an overdense region of the universe stops expanding, reaches its largest size, and begins to fall back in.
meanings.long: In the spherical collapse model the region is then about 5.6 times denser than the background. It collapses after twice the turnaround time and settles into a virialised halo.

meanings.short: A simple, exactly solvable model in which one uniform, slightly overdense sphere expands, stops, collapses and forms a halo.
meanings.long: Its two key numbers are still the working definitions of a halo: collapse happens when the linear density contrast reaches about 1.69, and the virialised halo is about 178 (18π²) times denser than the background. It follows the sphere as a small closed universe inside the background, using Birkhoff's theorem.

meanings.short: How much denser or thinner than average a region is, as a fraction of the average density.
meanings.long: It is δ = (ρ − ρ̄)/ρ̄. A region with δ > 0 is overdense, one with δ < 0 underdense. While δ is much less than one it grows in proportion to the growth factor; near one, non-linear collapse begins.

meanings.short: Following small departures from a smooth state by keeping only terms in the equations that are proportional to the departures, not their squares.
meanings.long: For density ripples it holds while the density contrast is much less than one; each Fourier mode then grows independently. Once δ approaches one the theory fails and collapse becomes non-linear.

meanings.short: Of the two solutions for a small density ripple, the one that grows with time; the other, the decaying mode, dies away.
meanings.long: In a matter-dominated universe the growing mode rises as the scale factor and the decaying mode falls as one over time, so after a while only the growing mode matters. In a radiation-dominated universe the growing mode rises as the square of the scale factor.

meanings.short: The factor D(t) by which small density ripples have grown since some starting time, set equal to one today.
meanings.long: In linear theory every large-scale ripple grows by the same factor, so δ = D δ₀. In a matter-dominated universe D grows in proportion to the scale factor; a cosmological constant slows it.

meanings.short: The factor by which sizes in the universe grew during inflation, e to the power of the number of e-foldings.
The collapse under its own gravity of a gas or star cloud larger than a certain size, because pressure can no longer hold it up.
meanings.long: Small ripples are pushed back by pressure or random motions and just oscillate as sound waves; ripples larger than the Jeans length grow. James Jeans worked it out in 1902.

meanings.short: The size above which a ripple in a self-gravitating gas collapses rather than oscillating: roughly the sound speed times the collapse time.
meanings.long: Its square is π times the sound speed squared over G times the density. Below it, pressure wins and the ripple is a sound wave; above it, gravity wins and the ripple grows.

meanings.short: The smallest mass that can collapse under its own gravity in a gas of given temperature and density: the mass inside a Jeans length.
meanings.long: For ordinary matter it fell dramatically at recombination, when the gas stopped being held up by radiation pressure. Cold dark matter, with tiny random speeds, has a tiny Jeans mass, so it can collapse on almost every scale.

meanings.short: The usual, strictly inconsistent step of assuming a uniform, static background has zero gravitational potential when deriving the Jeans instability.
meanings.long: Poisson's equation would then require zero density. The swindle gives the right answer anyway; in an expanding universe it is not needed, because the expansion supplies a consistent background.

meanings.short: Equations for the average motion of stars in a galaxy, like the fluid equations of a gas, with random star speeds acting as pressure.
meanings.long: They come from taking averages of the collisionless Boltzmann equation over velocity. For a steady, spherical system they give the mass inside each radius from the density and velocity dispersion of the stars, if the orbits' anisotropy is known.

meanings.short: A function giving how many stars (or particles) there are near each position with each velocity, at each time.
meanings.long: The number in a small box of positions and velocities is f times the box's size, d³x d³v. For stars that do not collide it obeys the collisionless Boltzmann equation, from which the Jeans equations follow.

meanings.short: A number β that says whether the stars of a galaxy move mostly in and out (radial orbits) or mostly round (circular orbits).
meanings.long: It is β = 1 − σ_t²/σ_r², comparing the spread of sideways and radial speeds. β = 0 means equal spreads, β near 1 nearly radial orbits, and negative β mostly circular ones.

meanings.short: The difficulty that the same observed star speeds can come from different masses with different orbit shapes, so mass and anisotropy cannot be separated.
meanings.long: Only speeds along the line of sight are measured, a mixture of radial and sideways motions. Without knowing the anisotropy β the Jeans equations do not give a unique mass, which is the main uncertainty of such estimates.

meanings.short: The speed at which small pressure disturbances travel through a material such as a gas; its square is the pressure change per density change.
meanings.long: In the early universe, while photons and baryons formed one fluid, it was about the speed of light divided by √3. After recombination it fell to a few kilometres per second, the speed of sound in ordinary warm hydrogen.

meanings.short: The test of whether a rotating disc of gas or stars will break into clumps: it is stable when the number Q is above one.
meanings.long: Q compares the random speeds of the disc with what is needed to resist collapse given its surface density and its rotation (through the epicycle frequency). Rotation holds up large scales and random motions small ones; when both fail, Q < 1, the disc fragments.

meanings.short: A simple method for predicting how many dark matter halos of each mass exist, from the statistics of the smoothed early density ripples.
meanings.long: William Press and Paul Schechter (1974) counted the fraction of space where the smoothed linear density contrast exceeds the collapse threshold, about 1.69. The simple version misses half the mass and is fixed with a factor of 2; the extended version explains why.

meanings.short: A refinement of the Press–Schechter method that follows the smoothed density as a random walk to count halos without missing any.
meanings.long: As the smoothing scale shrinks, the smoothed density at a point wanders; a point belongs to the largest halo whose threshold it first crosses. This solves the cloud-in-cloud problem and gives the factor of 2.

meanings.short: The flaw in the simple Press–Schechter count that a point below the threshold on one scale may still be inside a larger collapsed halo.
meanings.long: Such points are not counted, which is why the simple calculation finds only half the mass in halos. The extended Press–Schechter method fixes it by following each point through all smoothing scales.

meanings.short: The number of dark matter halos per unit volume in each range of mass, at a given time.
meanings.long: It is roughly a power law at low masses and falls exponentially above a characteristic mass that grows with time, as more and more large halos form. Press–Schechter theory predicts it from the early density ripples; simulations refine it.

meanings.short: A random pattern of values in space whose value at each point, and any combination of values, follows a bell-shaped normal distribution.
meanings.long: Such a field is described completely by its power spectrum. Inflation predicts that the early density ripples form one, which makes the statistics of halos calculable.

meanings.short: How much more likely than by chance it is to find two galaxies a given distance apart: zero for random placing, positive for clustering.
meanings.long: It is the average of the density contrast at one point times that at a point a distance r away. It is the Fourier transform of the power spectrum. For galaxies it falls as a power law, about r to the −1.8.

meanings.short: How much more strongly galaxies cluster than the matter as a whole; galaxies need not trace the mass exactly.
meanings.long: The bias b is the ratio of the galaxies' density ripples to those of all matter. Massive objects, which form only in the densest regions, are more strongly biased, so clusters cluster more than galaxies.

meanings.short: The early pattern of density ripples in which every scale has the same strength when it enters the horizon, so no size is special.
meanings.long: Its power spectrum is P(k) ∝ k, a power law with index n = 1. It was proposed around 1970, before inflation, which predicts a spectrum very close to it; measurements give n ≈ 0.96.

meanings.short: Existing from the very beginning, in the first moments of the universe, before later processes changed it.
meanings.long: The primordial power spectrum is the pattern of density ripples left at the end of inflation; primordial helium was made in the first minutes; primordial black holes would have formed before any star. The word stresses that something is a leftover from the early universe, not made later.

meanings.short: How strong the temperature ripples of the cosmic microwave background are at each angular size on the sky.
meanings.long: The sky map is broken into spherical harmonics; C_ℓ is the average squared strength at multipole ℓ, which corresponds to angles of about 180°/ℓ. Its peaks and plateau fix the curvature and contents of the universe.

origin: Greek an-, not, isos, equal, and tropos, direction.

meanings.short: A difference from one direction to another, such as the tiny temperature differences of the microwave background across the sky.
meanings.long: Primary anisotropies were set at the last scattering surface; secondary ones were added on the photons' way to us. The opposite is isotropy, being the same in every direction.

meanings.short: The velocity anisotropy β, which says whether stars or galaxies move mostly in and out or mostly round.
Temperature differences in the cosmic microwave background that were set at the time the light was released.
meanings.long: They include the Sachs–Wolfe and Doppler effects on large scales, the acoustic peaks from baryon acoustic oscillations, and Silk damping on the smallest scales. Their pattern on the sky carries most of what the microwave background tells about the universe's contents.

meanings.short: Temperature differences added to the cosmic microwave background on its way to us, after the light was released.
meanings.long: They come from scattering off electrons freed at reionization, from the integrated Sachs–Wolfe effect, from gravitational lensing and from the Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect in galaxy clusters. They are small compared with the primary ones on most scales, but carry information about later times.

meanings.short: The net temperature change of microwave light from a denser or thinner region: it loses energy climbing out, but comes from an earlier, hotter time.
meanings.long: Light leaving a potential well loses energy (gravitational redshift) but is also seen from a slightly earlier, hotter time. The first wins, so on large scales the wells look like slightly cold spots, with δT/T = Φ/3c².

meanings.short: The flat part of the microwave background's angular power spectrum at large angles, where only gravity had acted by recombination.
meanings.long: For a Harrison–Zel'dovich spectrum, ℓ(ℓ + 1)C_ℓ is roughly constant at multipoles below about 100, angles larger than the horizon at recombination. Its height measures the strength of the early density ripples on large scales.

meanings.short: A change in microwave background temperature from crossing gravitational wells that grow or fade while the light is passing through.
meanings.long: If a well did not change, the energy gained falling in would equal the energy lost climbing out. Dark energy makes large wells decay, so the light gains a little net energy.

meanings.short: The slight change in the microwave background seen through a galaxy cluster, as its hot gas scatters the light to higher energies.
meanings.long: Fast electrons in the cluster gas give some photons a kick, shifting the spectrum: fewer low-energy photons, more high-energy ones. It does not fade with distance, so it finds clusters far away.

meanings.short: The smoothing away of the smallest ripples in the early photon and baryon fluid, as photons diffuse out of them and drag the baryons along.
meanings.long: Below the Silk mass, about 10¹² solar masses, baryon ripples were erased before recombination; on the sky this damps the microwave background ripples smaller than a few arcminutes. Joseph Silk described it in 1968.

meanings.short: The stalling of dark matter clumps that come inside the horizon while radiation still dominates, because the expansion outpaces their collapse.
meanings.long: Such clumps grow only slowly, logarithmically, until matter–radiation equality, then grow in step with the scale factor. It bends the matter power spectrum on small scales. Péter Mészáros described it in 1974.

meanings.short: Sound waves in the early universe's mix of photons and ordinary matter, as gravity pulled it into wells and radiation pressure pushed it out.
meanings.long: They were frozen at recombination, leaving the acoustic peaks of the microwave background and a preferred separation of about 150 megaparsecs between galaxies today, a standard ruler for measuring the expansion. Galaxy surveys measure this ruler at different redshifts to trace the history of the expansion.

meanings.short: One of the peaks in the microwave background's angular power spectrum, from sound waves caught at maximum compression or rarefaction at recombination.
meanings.long: The first peak, near one degree, comes from waves that had just completed one compression. Its position measures the curvature of space, its height the matter density, and the height of the second relative to the first the baryon density.

meanings.short: The greatest distance a sound wave could have travelled in the early universe by a given time, usually the time of recombination.
meanings.long: With a sound speed of about c/√3 it is roughly the horizon divided by √3. Seen on the sky it sets the angle of the first acoustic peak, about one degree.

meanings.short: The effect of extra baryons on the sound waves of the early universe, like hanging a heavier mass on a spring.
meanings.long: The heavier fluid falls deeper into the wells but bounces back only as far, so compressions grow and rarefactions do not. The odd-numbered acoustic peaks are enhanced relative to the even ones, which measures the baryon density.

meanings.short: The push exerted by light or other radiation on matter, because photons carry momentum.
meanings.long: For radiation in equilibrium the pressure is one third of the energy density. In the early universe it held the baryons up against gravity; around a quasar it limits how fast gas can fall in.

meanings.short: A region where potential energy is lower than all around it, so matter or a particle tends to fall in and stay.
meanings.long: In cosmology the wells are dense clumps of dark matter: ordinary matter falls into them, and light climbing out of them is redshifted. Dark matter wells formed early and pulled in the ordinary matter after recombination.

meanings.short: The loss of energy, and lengthening of wavelength, of light climbing out of a gravitational field.
meanings.long: Light from a place of lower gravitational potential arrives with a longer wavelength: clocks there run slow compared with clocks higher up. It is one half of the Sachs–Wolfe effect.

meanings.short: The slowing of clocks deep in a gravitational field, so events there are seen as if they happened slightly earlier.
meanings.long: In the Sachs–Wolfe effect, a region inside a potential well is seen at a slightly earlier, hotter time. This partly cancels its gravitational redshift.

meanings.short: The bending of light by the gravity of mass along its path, which distorts, brightens or multiplies the images of objects behind.
meanings.long: General relativity predicts that light passing a mass M at distance b is bent by 4GM/(c²b). Lensing weighs all the mass in the lens, dark or not, whatever its motions. It ranges from strong lensing (rings, arcs, several images) to weak lensing (slight stretching).

meanings.short: The thin gas, mostly ionised hydrogen and helium, that fills the space between galaxies.
meanings.long: It holds most of the ordinary matter in the universe. Its absorption lines in quasar spectra, the Lyman-α forest, map its density, temperature and ionisation.

meanings.short: The strongest ultraviolet spectral line of hydrogen, at 121.6 nanometres, from an electron jumping between the lowest two energy levels.
meanings.long: Neutral hydrogen absorbs Lyman-α strongly, so even a little of it along the line of sight leaves a dark line in a quasar's spectrum, shifted by the expansion to a longer wavelength. It is the first line of the Lyman series; seen redshifted in distant gas, it falls in the visible range.

meanings.short: The many absorption lines in a distant quasar's spectrum made by clouds of hydrogen at different redshifts between it and us.
meanings.long: Each cloud absorbs Lyman-α at its own redshift, so its line lands at its own wavelength, always shorter than the quasar's own Lyman-α line. The forest is a one-dimensional map of the intergalactic gas.

meanings.short: A hydrogen cloud thick enough to absorb all the light that can ionise hydrogen; the thickest, damped systems, give very broad absorption lines.
meanings.long: Lyman-limit systems have column densities above about 10¹⁷ atoms per square centimetre and block all light shortward of 91.2 nanometres in their rest frame. Damped Lyman-α systems, above about 2 × 10²⁰, are probably the gas discs of young galaxies.

meanings.short: The number of atoms in a thin column through a cloud, per unit area of the column's cross-section, counted along the line of sight.
meanings.long: For hydrogen it is written N_HI, in atoms per square centimetre. The strength of an absorption line depends on it, not on the cloud's depth or density separately.

meanings.short: A measure of how strongly a medium absorbs or scatters light passing through it; transmitted light falls by a factor e to that power.
meanings.long: An optical depth much less than one means nearly transparent (optically thin); much more than one means nearly opaque (optically thick). For lensing the same name is used for the chance that a background star is magnified at a given moment.

meanings.short: A number that measures how strongly an atomic transition absorbs light, compared with an idealised classical oscillating electron.
meanings.long: The absorption cross-section of a line is proportional to it. For hydrogen's Lyman-α line it is about 0.42.

meanings.short: Hydrogen atoms with their electron still attached, as opposed to ionised hydrogen, which has lost it.
meanings.long: Astronomers write it HI (said 'H one') and ionised hydrogen HII. Neutral hydrogen absorbs Lyman-α and gives off the 21-centimetre radio line.

meanings.short: The share of hydrogen atoms that are neutral rather than ionised.
meanings.long: It is X_HI = n_HI / n_H. In the intergalactic medium since reionization it is only about one in 100,000, held down by the ultraviolet background.

meanings.short: The knocking of an electron out of an atom by a photon with enough energy; for hydrogen it needs ultraviolet light above 13.6 electronvolts.
meanings.long: In the intergalactic medium the ultraviolet background photoionizes each hydrogen atom far faster than electrons and protons can recombine, which keeps the gas almost fully ionized. The atoms recombine only slowly, because the gas is so thin.

meanings.short: The combined ultraviolet light of all galaxies and quasars that fills intergalactic space.
meanings.long: It keeps the intergalactic gas ionized and hot. It can also stop small galaxies forming stars, by heating the gas in their shallow potential wells.

meanings.short: The era, roughly 0.2 to 1 billion years after the Big Bang, when light from the first stars and quasars ionized intergalactic hydrogen again.
meanings.long: After recombination the gas was neutral. Ultraviolet light from the first sources ionized it again, a process complete by a redshift of about 6. Its end shows as the Gunn–Peterson trough in the most distant quasars.

meanings.short: The complete absorption of a quasar's light at wavelengths shorter than its Lyman-α line, expected if the gas in between is mostly neutral.
meanings.long: James Gunn and Bruce Peterson (1965) showed that even a tiny neutral fraction, spread smoothly, would absorb everything. Quasars below a redshift of about 6 show only a forest of lines, so the gas is almost fully ionised; beyond 6 the trough appears.

meanings.short: A very bright galaxy centre powered by gas falling into a supermassive black hole, visible across most of the universe.
meanings.long: A quasar can outshine its whole galaxy a thousand times over from a region smaller than the Solar System. Strictly, quasars are radio-loud and QSOs (quasi-stellar objects) radio-quiet; both look like stars in images.

meanings.short: The centre of a galaxy that gives off huge amounts of light not made by stars, powered by a supermassive black hole swallowing gas.
meanings.long: AGN (said A-G-N) shine across the spectrum from radio to X-rays and can vary within days, which shows the source is tiny. Quasars, Seyfert galaxies, radio galaxies and BL Lac objects are kinds of AGN.

meanings.short: A black hole of a million to ten billion solar masses, found at the centre of most large galaxies.
meanings.long: Gas falling into one heats up in an accretion disc and can shine as an active galactic nucleus. Their masses grow with the velocity dispersion of their host galaxies' bulges, a sign that black hole and galaxy grew together.

origin: Latin accrescere, to grow by additions.

meanings.short: The growth of an object by gas or matter falling onto it under gravity.
meanings.long: Accretion onto a black hole turns gravitational energy into heat and light very efficiently, about a tenth of the rest energy in the notes' estimate a sixteenth. Halos also grow by accretion of smooth dark matter as well as by mergers.

meanings.short: A flat, spinning disc of gas spiralling into a black hole or star, heated by friction until it glows.
meanings.long: Gas cannot fall straight in because it carries angular momentum; viscosity in the disc lets it drift inwards and converts its energy into heat and light. Around a supermassive black hole the disc shines in ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light.

meanings.short: The smallest stable circular orbit around a black hole; closer in, matter soon plunges in.
meanings.long: For a non-spinning black hole it lies at three Schwarzschild radii. It marks the inner edge of an accretion disc and sets how much energy the gas can radiate before it falls in.

meanings.short: The greatest luminosity an object can have before the push of its own light on infalling gas beats the pull of its gravity.
meanings.long: It is 4πGMm_p c divided by the Thomson cross-section, about 1.3 × 10³⁸ erg per second per solar mass. A quasar's luminosity therefore sets a lower limit to its black hole's mass.

meanings.short: The rate of feeding whose released energy equals the Eddington luminosity, roughly the fastest steady rate at which a black hole can swallow gas.
meanings.long: Faster infall would produce more light, whose pressure would push the gas back. Simulations cap black hole growth at this rate.

meanings.short: The idea that the different kinds of active galactic nucleus are one kind of object seen from different directions and feeding at different rates.
meanings.long: A black hole with an accretion disc, jets, a dusty torus and clouds of gas looks like a quasar seen face-on, like a narrow-line galaxy when the torus hides the centre, and like a BL Lac object when a jet points at us. Different accretion rates explain further differences, such as between radio-loud and radio-quiet objects.

meanings.short: A thick ring of dust around the centre of an active galaxy, which hides the central engine when seen edge-on and glows in the infrared.
meanings.long: It reaches from about one to about a hundred parsecs from the black hole. It absorbs ultraviolet and optical light and re-emits it as infrared.

meanings.short: The clouds of gas close to an active galaxy's black hole, moving so fast that their spectral lines are widened by thousands of km/s.
meanings.long: It lies within about a parsec of the black hole and moves at about 10,000 km/s. Farther out, slower clouds of the narrow-line region give narrower lines. Whether the broad lines are seen depends on whether the dusty torus hides them.

meanings.short: A narrow, fast beam of gas shot out from near a black hole, sometimes reaching far beyond its galaxy.
meanings.long: Jets carry particles at nearly light speed in opposite directions along the black hole's axis. Their electrons, spiralling in magnetic fields, give off radio light; where they end they inflate the lobes of radio galaxies.

meanings.short: An active galaxy that shines very brightly in radio waves, usually from two huge lobes fed by jets from its centre.
meanings.long: The lobes can reach millions of light-years from the galaxy. Electrons accelerated in them give off synchrotron radiation.

meanings.short: A spiral galaxy with a bright, compact active nucleus, less powerful than a quasar.
meanings.long: Named after Carl Seyfert, who described them in 1943. Their nuclei give off 10⁴² to 10⁴⁵ erg per second and show strong emission lines.

meanings.short: An active galaxy whose jet points almost straight at us, so it looks extremely bright, varies quickly and its light is strongly polarised.
meanings.long: Named after the first one found, BL Lacertae, at first taken for a variable star. Its spectrum shows few emission lines, because the beamed light of the jet drowns them.

meanings.short: Light given off by electrons moving at nearly light speed as they spiral around magnetic field lines.
meanings.long: It dominates the radio light of jets, lobes and supernova remnants. Its smooth spectrum and polarisation distinguish it from the light of stars or hot gas.

meanings.short: The number of baryons (protons and neutrons) for each photon in the universe, about six for every ten billion photons.
meanings.long: It is written η. It has not changed since the first minutes, and it sets how much deuterium and helium Big Bang nucleosynthesis made, so measuring those fixes the baryon density.

meanings.short: Heavy hydrogen: hydrogen whose nucleus, the deuteron, holds a neutron as well as a proton.
meanings.long: The deuteron is held together by only 2.22 MeV, so it was easily broken apart in the hot early universe. The deuterium left over from the Big Bang depends sensitively on the baryon density, which makes it the best measure of it.

meanings.short: The delay at the start of Big Bang nucleosynthesis while deuterium, the first step, kept being broken up by the many energetic photons.
meanings.long: There are about a billion photons per baryon, so even when typical photons were far too weak, enough in the high-energy tail could split each deuteron formed. Deuterium survived only once the temperature fell well below 2.22 MeV, after which helium formed quickly.

meanings.short: The share of the mass of ordinary matter in helium-4, about a quarter from the Big Bang.
meanings.long: It is written Y. Almost every neutron left when the deuterium bottleneck opened ended up in helium, so Y depends mainly on the ratio of neutrons to protons then, about one to seven.

meanings.short: The average time an unstable particle survives before decaying; after one mean lifetime about 37 per cent of a sample is left.
meanings.long: It is the time τ in the exponential decay law N = N₀ e^(−t/τ). The half-life is shorter, τ ln 2, about 0.69 τ. A free neutron's mean lifetime is about 880 seconds.

meanings.short: The small fraction of particles or photons in a thermal distribution with energies far above the average.
meanings.long: It falls off exponentially but never vanishes. With a billion photons per baryon, the tail of the black-body spectrum held enough energetic photons to delay nucleosynthesis long after typical photons became too weak.

origin: Greek galaxias, milky, from the Milky Way.

meanings.short: A huge system of stars, gas and dust, from thousands to over a trillion stars, held together by gravity inside a dark matter halo.
meanings.long: Our own galaxy, the Milky Way, is written with a capital: the Galaxy. The 8.902 notes define a galaxy as stars and dark matter, which behave as a collisionless fluid, orbiting together with gas, which does collide, in the potential they make together.

meanings.short: The explosion of a star at the end of its life, briefly as bright as a whole galaxy.
meanings.long: Massive stars explode when their cores collapse; white dwarfs explode when they gain too much mass (type Ia). Supernovae spread the heavy elements made in stars, and their energy, about 10⁵¹ erg each, heats and drives out gas, slowing star formation (supernova feedback).

meanings.short: MOND: a proposal to change Newton's law of gravity at very small accelerations instead of adding dark matter.
meanings.long: Proposed by Mordecai Milgrom in 1983, it keeps Newton's law at large accelerations but makes gravity stronger below about 10⁻¹⁰ m/s². It explains flat rotation curves and the Tully–Fisher relation, but struggles with galaxy clusters and the cosmic microwave background.

meanings.short: At shorter wavelengths than a given line in a spectrum, towards the blue end; also called blue-ward.
meanings.long: In a quasar's spectrum the Lyman-α forest lies short-ward of the quasar's own Lyman-α line, because each absorbing cloud lies closer to us and so at lower redshift. Because redshift moves lines to longer wavelengths, lower-redshift absorbers appear short-ward.
